title: Wavefunction-templated metamaterials
authors: Yutao Chen, Tao Xiao, Jing Li, Aodong Li, Biye Xie
abstract: Metamaterials, which store, guide and emit waves through their eigenmodes, have enabled the development of devices with unprecedented functionalities. Yet the spatial profiles of conventional metamaterials' eigenmodes are typically determined by their pre-determined structures (Hamiltonians). In this work, we introduce `wavefunction-templated metamaterials', a class of physically realizable metamaterials hosting diverse prescribed, spectrally isolated eigenstates. The resulting Hamiltonian geometries obey a boundary law, with the required nonlocality determined solely by single-contact boundary sites, independent of the state interior or lattice size. The sparse Hamiltonians are then Hermitianized, followed by spectral reshaping to open a protective gap around the target eigenstate. We validate our approach in discrete lattices and acoustic metamaterials. Although demonstrated in acoustics, the principle can be applied to thermal, electrical-circuit and photonic metamaterials.
summary: This paper introduces 'wavefunction-templated metamaterials,' a method to engineer physical structures whose eigenstates match a user-defined spatial profile. By controlling the Hamiltonian's sparsity and spectral parameters, the authors successfully demonstrated the realization and spectral isolation of these target states in both theoretical lattices and physical acoustic systems.
main_problem: The core problem is to reverse the conventional design paradigm in metamaterials: instead of designing a structure (Hamiltonian) to yield specific eigenmodes, the authors aim to prescribe a desired field distribution ($\psi_0$) and engineer a physically realizable structure that hosts it as a spectrally isolated eigenstate.
main_result: They established a framework to realize gap-isolated eigenstates with arbitrary spatial profiles in sparse, physically implementable Hamiltonians, successfully demonstrating this concept in both discrete lattice models and continuum acoustic metamaterials.
method: The method involves constructing a sparse Hamiltonian that enforces local destructive-interference conditions dictated by the target wavefunction, followed by spectral reshaping within a parameterized subspace to open a protective spectral gap.
model_or_system: The system is modeled using tight-binding Hamiltonians on discrete lattices, applicable to photonic, acoustic, thermal, and electrical-circuit metamaterials. The concept was extended to full-wave simulations of acoustic metamaterials fabricated via 3D printing.
key_observables: Spectral gap ($g(	heta)$), the field distribution of the eigenstate ($\psi_0$), and the measured acoustic pressure response ($P_{in}(f)$ vs $P_{out}(f)$).
important_parameters: The required nonlocality is determined solely by the number of 'single-contact (SC) boundary sites,' independent of the lattice size.
main_assumptions: The construction relies on enforcing local destructive-interference conditions, and the continuum transition required imposing an additional constraint on on-site energies.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the Hamiltonian construction, spectral gap opening, and the successful experimental observation of prescribed orbital-like states (S, P, D, CUHK) in fabricated acoustic metamaterials.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from theoretical formulation in discrete lattices (Hamiltonian construction, spectral reshaping) to numerical validation, and finally to experimental realization and measurement in physical acoustic metamaterials.
why_interesting: This work provides a powerful, constructive tool for designing quantum/wave systems by specifying the desired quantum state rather than the underlying physical geometry, which is highly relevant for quantum optics and engineered wave dynamics.
